transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2027-04-15 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Tomás (Redwood SE), Aisha (Sentinel CTO), Miguel (Lead ML), Lina (Infra)

Summary (auto): deep dive into p95/p99 tail latency impacting teleop control loop; focus on streaming responses and network pathing.

00:00 Jared: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, uh we'll jump right in. quick intros?
00:06 Aisha: yep Aisha here, CTO, Miguel is lead on inference, Lina handles infra and on-prem networking.
00:12 Priya: hi all, Priya SE from Redwood, Tomás and I will run through the latency profile and dig into p95/p99 causes.
00:20 Miguel: appreciate it. high level we see spikes in p99 around 400-550ms for short sequences (<=64 tokens) which is surprising — baseline p50 is 40ms.
00:30 Tomás: ok noted, can you share observed distribution? sequences, batch sizes, streaming vs non- streaming?
00:37 Miguel: mostly streaming, small seqs 16-64, we also do some batched bulk for analytics but teleop is streaming single-request. batch size at client is 1-2 usually.
00:45 Priya: alr, so two immediate axes: model runtime tail (KV cache misses, kernel stalls) and network hops (cross-AZ, NAT, TLS handshakes). We'll walk through server-side traces and network traces.
01:02 Lina: most of our infra is in us-west-2, we have a VPC with peered on-prem via vpn, and some requests go through a bastion/NAT. suspecting the vpn/policy is adding jitter.
01:15 Jared: yeah ok, let's start with runtime — Priya do you want to share the profile?
01:20 Priya: sure, I'll summarize — our runtime has a few hotspots: token generation GPU time, kernel launch overhead for small seqs, and KV cache warmup on model sharding. for streaming we flush partial tokens which can increase syscall frequency.
01:38 Priya: (note: transcription may mangle some kernel names) we instrumented on A100 and H100. p50 GPU time per token is 10-12ms for the model they're using (Redwood-curated 7B variant), p95 jumps to ~90ms in bad cases, p99 up to 400ms when KV cache cold or when the request hits a shard that didn't have warmed KV.
02:01 Miguel: hmm we thought KV cache would avoid most of that, are we seeing cache eviction?
02:06 Priya: yes for short bursty traffic KV cache eviction can happen if the shard memory is tight and sequence length variance causes inconsistent cache hits, also continuous batching can cause re-ordering that invalidates prefetched prefixes.
02:18 Tomás: another nuance is kernel selection overhead — for 1-2 token outputs the runtime sometimes picks a default path that has higher latency; we can force a lightweight fast-path for short sequences.
02:30 Aisha: would that change quality? we can't have hallucinations due to aggressive quantization or kernel changes.
02:36 Priya: good point — quantization (8-bit/4-bit) can change numeric stability; we typically test for regressions. For p99 reduction we often prefer algorithmic changes first (cache warmup, routing) before lowering precision.
02:50 Miguel: can you explain streaming vs non-streaming diff? we assumed streaming always adds overhead because of many small writes.
02:56 Priya: streaming adds small chattiness — there is per-chunk framing + TLS record overhead + application flushes. Non-streaming composes full response server-side then sends; that can reduce per-token latency but increases tail for longer sequences if server waits. For teleop short tokens streaming can be beneficial but only if network and server path are optimized for small packets.
03:18 Lina: we saw large variance correlated with a specific NAT gateway in our VPC — when traffic egresses through that gateway p99 jumps 200-300ms.
03:27 Jared: that matches what we see in customer networks — cross-AZ and NAT gateways are big contributors. we sometimes recommend colocating edge proxies or using dedicated peering.
03:35 Miguel: what's the cost tradeoff of dedicated peering vs hosted public endpoint?
03:40 Tomás: dedicated peering reduces network hop latency and jitter. cost depends on volume and region egress. We'll include cost/latency projection in the follow-up.
03:49 Priya: back to runtime: we recommend profiling tok/sec per GPU for their model variant. if they use continuous batching, tune max batch size and max latency buffer so tiny single-request fast-paths bypass big kernels.
04:05 Miguel: what's a realistic fast-path config?
04:09 Priya: e.g., max_batch_size 8, latency_ms 20, and a separate route for low-latency calls with batch size 1 and priority scheduling. Also enable KV prefix pinning for teleop prefixes to keep them resident.
04:25 Aisha: prefix pinning? explain.
04:28 Priya: you can instruct the runtime to keep certain prefixes (common command sequences) in KV cache and mark them as hot — reduces warmup. downside is memory usage per shard increases.
04:39 Miguel: ok memory is available but we'd like automatic eviction policies. do you have those?
04:44 Tomás: yes LRU with weights, and we surface eviction metrics. we can also set a reserve pool for pinned prefixes.
04:52 Priya: another runtime trick is artificial batching windows — group single-requests for X ms to increase GPU utilization but that increases p50 slightly, need to find sweet spot for p99.
05:05 Miguel: how do you measure and attribute p99 to network vs runtime? we only see overall latency in app logs.
05:12 Priya: you need distributed tracing — instrument at client (request send), edge proxy, runtime ingress, and GPU timestamps. Redwood's tracing breaks down network, runtime scheduling, queue time, GPU compute, and post-processing. Sampled traces for p99 are important.
05:29 Miguel: can you share an example trace?
05:31 Priya: yes we'll share a sample with the benchmarking template. typical p99 trace for our customers often shows 40-60ms network jitter, 150-300ms runtime gap when cache is cold, and 50-100ms kernel overhead in some cases.
05:45 Lina: we need to understand cross-AZ when using on-prem peering — is TLS termination done at Redwood edge or at peering?
05:52 Jared: for hosted endpoints TLS terminates at Redwood edge. for private/VPC we can offer TLS passthrough and also bring-your-own-terminator if you want termination in your VPC.
06:03 Aisha: that would let us avoid double-encryption overhead on the VPN.
06:08 Priya: yes and also reduces CPU overhead on the path; TLS handshake can add 50-120ms if not re-used. keep connections alive, use HTTP/2 or QUIC to reduce handshake overhead.
06:20 Miguel: QUIC support?
06:22 Tomás: experimental, but QUIC can reduce tail latency on lossy networks. we use HTTP/2 in most clients though.
06:29 Miguel: how does KV cache warm start work in autoscaled dedicated capacity? when a new worker spins up it starts cold, that's hurting us.
06:35 Priya: autoscaling brings cold workers — for critical routes we recommend pre-warming policies and reserved capacity. Redwood Dedicated lets you reserve a pool with pinned KV snapshots that can be loaded quickly.
06:48 Aisha: snapshots — are those persisted to S3 or similar and how long to load?
06:53 Tomás: snapshots are stored in fast object store; loading depends on model size and network, typically 500ms-2s for large models; for 7B variants it's faster (100-400ms). but loading is parallelized across shards.
07:08 Miguel: 500ms load is still bad for teleop p99.
07:11 Priya: yes we use strategies: keep small reserved pool, or maintain warm standby replicas for latency-critical routes. standbys cost more but ensure low tail.
07:22 Miguel: about quantization — we test 8-bit and 4-bit. how much p99 improvement do you see? and any accuracy regressions?
07:30 Priya: quantization reduces memory pressure and can reduce kernel runtime by 10-40% depending on kernel and hardware. p99 can drop significantly if memory-induced eviction is the main cause. accuracy-wise 8-bit usually safe for many models; 4-bit needs evals — for teleop you must run safety tests.
07:46 Lina: which hardware do you recommend? we have options for H100 and A100 on dedicated pools.
07:51 Tomás: H100 generally better for large throughput and mixed precision kernels; for small-seq latency differences may be smaller. H100's faster memory bandwidth helps KV-heavy workloads. A100 is cost-effective and still good.
08:04 Miguel: can you give an example: our profile p50=40ms p95=140ms p99=450ms on H100 — what's realistic reduction with warm KV and fast-path?
08:13 Priya: with pinned prefixes, fast-path and reduced network hops we often see p95 under 80-120ms and p99 under 180-220ms for similar workloads. If kv cold or cross-AZ issues remain you'll still see spikes.
08:27 Aisha: what about streaming chunk size? we stream very small chunks.
08:31 Priya: increase chunk size to 32-64 bytes or use application-level coalescing — fewer TLS records per response helps. also ensure Nagle is disabled on certain paths to avoid delays in coalescing.
08:45 Miguel: any infra-level network tuning you recommend?
08:48 Lina: we control MTU and path MTU; also ensure ENA drivers up to date on EC2, use placement groups to reduce cross-host latency. Also consider private link or direct connect to reduce internet jitter.
09:02 Tomás: and set TCP keepalive high so TLS sessions are reused; ephemeral TLS sessions cause handshake cost.
09:08 Jared: we should also talk about tracing sample rates — for p99 you need 100% sampling for short windows or spike detection otherwise you'll miss the event.
09:18 Miguel: ok noted. any suggestions on per- request instrumentation cost? we worry about overhead.
09:23 Priya: sample at 1% normally, bump to 100% for suspected windows using dynamic sampling. traces are lightweight if you only record timestamps and IDs not full payloads.
09:35 Miguel: how about queueing and backpressure? we saw queue bursts when autoscaler spins up.
09:40 Priya: queue time is often the silent killer — if ingress queue is long you get head-of-line blocking. use multiple ingress queues per priority tier and preempt lower priority. Also set request-level deadlines and cancellation.
09:55 Aisha: can Redwood runtime preempt long-running background batches in favor of low-latency teleop?
09:59 Tomás: yes with priority scheduling; background batch lanes are lower priority and can be bumped when high-priority arrives. it's a configurable policy.
10:09 Miguel: curious about the impact of model sharding — sometimes a token touches multiple shards and there are cross-shard syncs.
10:15 Priya: cross-shard synchronization adds latency; we use async KV merging and do as much local compute as possible. model parallelism choices matter; for 7B models you usually fit on single GPU and avoid cross-shard comms. larger models incur more cross-gpu overhead.
10:33 Miguel: good, we're using a 13B variant in some pipelines for reasoning — might be more affected.
10:38 Priya: yep 13B will have more kernel and cross-device overhead. options: quantize, pipeline parallelism tuning, or pick smaller variant for teleop.
10:48 Aisha: can you summarize recommended immediate actions for us?
10:52 Priya: sure — 1) capture distributed traces for next 72 hours at higher sampling focusing on teleop endpoints; 2) provide sequence length distro and client chunk sizes; 3) try prefix pinning for top 20 commands in a staging bucket; 4) consider reserved capacity or warm standbys for teleop route; 5) test 8-bit quantization in eval harness for safety and perf.
11:15 Miguel: we'll do that, we'll also export CDN/NAT logs.
11:18 Jared: quick technical aside — we saw p99 bump when Kubernetes node gets CPU steal from noisy neighbors due to TLS offload; in dedicated pools we isolate CPUs for networking.
11:30 Lina: on our on-prem side we have an L7 load balancer in front of the VPN, might add jitter. Would a direct VPC endpoint help?
11:36 Tomás: yes, a VPC endpoint with private link or direct connect reduces external hops; we'll outline network topologies in the follow-up doc.
11:45 Miguel: any automation we can use for warm cache?
11:48 Priya: yes, Redwood supports a warmup script that replays representative prefixes into the cache on deploy or scale events. It can be part of the rollout pipeline.
11:57 Aisha: how about monitoring — what dashboards should we watch to catch tail events early?
12:03 Priya: p95/p99 by endpoint, KV hit rate, cache eviction rate, queue time histograms, kernel latency histograms, network egress latency per gateway, TLS handshake counts. alert on sudden drop in KV hit rate or queue time above threshold.
12:18 Miguel: ok great. last question: what's the expected improvement if we move teleop endpoints to Dedicated vs stay Hosted?
12:25 Tomás: Dedicated with reserved capacity, pinned KV and peering usually eliminates a lot of network jitter and cold-starts; you can expect more predictable p99 (range 150-250ms) vs hosted public endpoints which vary more depending on network path. cost and ops tradeoffs apply.
12:41 Aisha: we need a cost/latency tradeoff sheet.
12:44 Jared: we'll include that.
12:46 Priya: wrapping up — we'll send the benchmark template, sample traces, recommended runtime config patch, and follow-up scheduling link.
12:54 Miguel: thanks all, appreciate the run-through.
12:58 Aisha: thanks, bye.
13:00 Jared: thanks everyone, bye.

Notes: transcript includes crosstalk and occasional mis- spelled technical terms (quantizashun, K-V cash) as typical of auto-transcribe.
